title: Planning regulation application, effectiveness, and delegated powers
mainQuestion: How do section 125 planning regulations apply across areas and local governments, and what effects or delegated powers can follow?
studySummary: Section 125(2) to 125(9) combines several distinct rules: payment of prescribed development-approval fees, area designation for regulation application, limits and exceptions for municipal, village, rural-community, local-government, and local-service-district effectiveness, priority for land-use policy regulations, consistency with rural plans, and development-officer or regional-service-commission powers. Because these rules cover several separate recall topics, the group should be split before approval as a single study unit.

objectives.objective: Recall where prescribed paragraph 125(1)(h) fees are paid and credited.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Where must a prescribed fee under paragraph 125(1)(h) be paid and credited?
objectives.studyAnswer: If a fee is prescribed under paragraph 125(1)(h), it shall be paid, despite the Financial Administration Act, to the regional service commission and credited to the cost of delivering the land use planning service under subsection 161(4) of the Local Governance Act.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(2)If a fee is prescribed under paragraph (1)(h), the fee shall be paid, despite the Financial Administration Act, to the regional service commission and shall be credited to the cost of the delivery of the land use planning service under subsection 161(4) of the Local Governance Act.

objectives.objective: Recall how the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may define the area where a section 125 regulation applies.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How may the Lieutenant-Governor in Council restrict or extend the area of application for a section 125 regulation?
objectives.studyAnswer: Subject to subsections 125(4) and 125(7), the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may designate areas for the application of a section 125 regulation, except for a rural plan under section 51, and may provide that a subdivision regulation applies throughout the Province except areas identified as not subject to it.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(3)Subject to subsections (4) and (7), the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may (a) except in the case of a rural plan under section 51, designate an area or areas for the purpose of the application of a regulation under this section, thereby restricting, subject to paragraph (b), the application of the regulation accordingly, and (b) with respect to a subdivision regulation, provide that the regulation applies throughout the Province exclusive of those areas identified in the regulation as not being subject to the regulation.

objectives.objective: Recall the local effectiveness rules for section 125 regulations.
objectives.guidedQuestion: When is a section 125 regulation ineffective or effective in municipalities, villages, rural communities, local governments, and local service districts?
objectives.studyAnswer: A section 125 regulation is generally not effective in a municipality, but a paragraph 125(1)(a) or 125(1)(f) regulation is effective in a village within its area if the specified zoning, rural-plan, or subdivision by-law is not in effect. It is not effective in a rural community with a by-law on the same matter. Despite that, a paragraph 125(1)(j) regulation is effective in a local government or local service district specified in the regulation.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(4)A regulation under this section (a) subject to paragraph (b), is not effective in a municipality; (b) if made under paragraph (1)(a) or (f), is effective in a village that is within an area in which it applies and (i) in the case of a regulation under paragraph (1)(a), no zoning by-law or zoning provisions in a rural plan under section 33 are in effect in the village, or (ii) in the case of a regulation under paragraph (1)(f), no subdivision by-law is in effect in the village; and (c) is not effective in a rural community that has a by-law in effect respecting the same matter as the regulation. 125(5)Despite subsection (4), a regulation under paragraph (1)(j) is effective in a local government or local service district specified in the regulation.

objectives.objective: Recall the priority and rural-plan consistency rules for section 125 regulations.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How do section 125 regulations interact with land-use plans and other instruments?
objectives.studyAnswer: If a paragraph 125(1)(j) regulation is inconsistent with a regional land use plan, rural plan, municipal plan, by-law, or regulation under the Act, except a regulation establishing a statement of public interest, the paragraph 125(1)(j) regulation prevails. A section 125 regulation applicable in an area designated under subsection 125(3) or paragraph 52(1)(a) shall be consistent with any rural plan in effect in the area.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(6)Despite any other provision in this Act, if there is an inconsistency between a regulation under paragraph (1)(j) and a regional land use plan, rural plan, municipal plan or by-law or regulation under this Act, except a regulation establishing a statement of public interest, the regulation under paragraph (1)(j) prevails. 125(7)With respect to a regulation made under this section applicable in an area designated under subsection (3) or paragraph 52(1)(a), the regulation shall be consistent with a rural plan, if any, in effect in the area.

objectives.objective: Recall who acts as development officer and what zoning-related powers may be vested or deemed vested.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What development-officer and regional-service-commission powers can arise when a section 125 regulation is in effect?
objectives.studyAnswer: If a section 125 regulation is in effect, the planning director as defined in the Regional Services Delivery Act is the development officer, and listed powers are deemed vested in the regional service commission. For a zoning regulation or zoning provisions in a rural plan, subsection 125(9) allows or deems specified land-use, variance, fee, and rezoning-related powers to be vested in the regional service commission, the relevant development officer, or the Minister as stated.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(8)If a regulation under this section is in effect, the planning director as defined in the Regional Services Delivery Act is the development officer and the powers vested in a regional service commission under paragraph (9)(a) or (e), (10)(b) or (11)(b) shall be deemed to be vested in the regional service commission. 125(9)With respect to a zoning regulation or to zoning provisions in a rural plan under this section (a) the powers and functions referred to in paragraphs 53(2)(g), (g.1) and (h) or paragraph 53(3)(c), with respect to particular uses of land, may be vested in a regional service commission, (b) if the power referred to in subparagraph 53(2)(i)(ii) is provided for in the regulation, a letter from the Minister shall satisfy the requirement of clause 53(2)(i)(ii)(C), (c) the power referred to in paragraph 53(2)(j) may be vested in a regional service commission and, if it is, subsection 53(9) applies with the necessary modifications to the regulation, (d) if a fee referred to in paragraph 53(2)(l) is provided for in the regulation, it shall be paid into the Consolidated Fund, but may be returned in whole or in part on the advice of the Minister, (e) the powers referred to in sections 55 and 56 with respect to certain proposed uses and variances shall be deemed to be vested in the relevant regional service commission or development officer, as the case may be, and (f) if a person applies to the Minister to have an area of land re-zoned to permit the carrying out of a specific proposal, (i) the Minister, in relation to the application, may make an order or enter into an agreement with the person, and (ii) the provisions of section 59 with respect to a resolution or agreement under that section apply with the necessary modifications to an order or agreement made under this section.

title: Subdivision public-purpose land, money, procedure, summary, and filing rules
mainQuestion: What public-purpose, procedural, summary, and filing rules apply to subdivision and other regulations under section 125?
studySummary: Subsections 125(10) to 125(16) cover several separate topics: what a subdivision regulation may provide, how subdivision by-law provisions and variance powers apply, how Crown-held public-purpose land and money in lieu of land are handled, what the Minister must do before making a regulation, when a written summary can stand in for public consideration of a proposed rural plan or amendment, and where the Director files regulations. The group is too broad for one approvable recall unit.

objectives.objective: Recall what a subdivision regulation may provide for public-purpose land, money, powers, fees, street naming, and exemptions.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What matters may a subdivision regulation under section 125 address?
objectives.studyAnswer: A subdivision regulation may provide for setting aside public-purpose land, money in lieu of that land at the Minister discretion, regional service commission powers over access and subdivision-plan approval, tentative-plan approval fees, regional service commission approval of subdivision street names, and added exemptions for land in the regulation area.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(10)A subdivision regulation under this section may (a) subject to subsections (12) and (13), provide for (i) the setting aside of land for public purposes at a location as may be approved by the Minister after consultation with the regional service commission, the indicating of the land on a subdivision plan and the vesting of the land in the Crown on the filing of the subdivision plan in the land registration office, and (ii) the paying, at the discretion of the Minister, of money in lieu of land mentioned in subparagraph (i), (b) vest in a regional service commission the power referred to in paragraph 75(1)(c) with respect to access, (c) vest in a regional service commission the power referred to in paragraph 75(1)(k) with respect to approval of a subdivision plan, (d) prescribe the fee to be paid for the approval of a tentative plan, including prescribing different fees for the approval of tentative plans for type 1 subdivisions and type 2 subdivisions, (e) provide that the naming of streets in subdivisions is subject to the approval of the regional service commission, and (f) add to the list of exemptions referred to in subsection 80(1) with respect to land in the area to which the regulation applies.

objectives.objective: Recall how subdivision by-law provisions apply when a subdivision regulation is in effect.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What procedural rules apply when a subdivision regulation under section 125 is in effect?
objectives.studyAnswer: Section 77 applies with necessary modifications, except that a plan involving public-purpose land shall not be approved unless the regional service commission has recommended the land location and the Minister has approved and signed the plan. Section 78 variance powers are vested in the regional service commission or development officer, and sections 79 and 80 apply with necessary modifications.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(11)If a subdivision regulation under this section is in effect, (a) the provisions of section 77 with respect to a subdivision by-law apply with the necessary modifications to the regulation, except if a plan involves the setting aside of land for public purposes, in which case the plan shall not be approved unless (i) the location of the land has been recommended by the regional service commission, and (ii) the plan has been approved and signed by the Minister, (b) the powers mentioned in section 78 with respect to variance are vested in the regional service commission or development officer, as the case may be, and (c) sections 79 and 80 apply with the necessary modifications to the regulation.

objectives.objective: Recall how land and money for public purposes are held and used.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How must public-purpose land and money in lieu of that land be handled under section 125?
objectives.studyAnswer: Land vested in the Crown shall be held undeveloped or developed for public purposes, may later be conveyed to a local government if included within its boundaries, and is subject to the Act provisions affecting public-purpose land vested in a local government. Money received in lieu of land or from sale of land goes to a special account and may be spent only to acquire or develop land for public purposes, with investment earnings added and remaining amounts paid to a later-included local government as stated.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(12)Land vested in the Crown under this section shall be held undeveloped or developed for public purposes and may, if subsequently included within the boundaries of a local government, be conveyed to the local government and the land shall be subject to all provisions of this Act affecting land for public purposes vested in a local government under this Act. 125(13)All money received by the Minister in lieu of land for public purposes or realized by the Minister on the sale of the land is to be paid into a special account, and the money in that account is to be expended by the Minister for acquiring or developing land for public purposes and for no other purpose, and (a) pending the expenditure the money shall be invested and the earnings derived from the investments paid into the special account, and (b) if a subdivision in respect of which money has been received is subsequently included within the boundaries of a local government, the portion of the money that remains unexpended, together with any increments that have accrued under paragraph (a), is to be paid to the local government of which the subdivision becomes a part, and is to be treated by the local government in the same manner as money received for a public purpose under a subdivision by-law.

objectives.objective: Recall pre-making consultation and public-consideration procedure for section 125 regulations.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must the Minister do before making a regulation under section 125, and what written-summary exception applies?
objectives.studyAnswer: Before making a section 125 regulation, the Minister shall request regional service commission views if the regulation would affect a region, request advisory committee views for a section 51 regulation affecting a rural district with an advisory committee, and follow the section 111 preliminary by-law procedure with necessary modifications, except for regulations under paragraph 125(1)(a), (b), (f), or (g). For a zoning regulation under subsection 125(1) or a rural plan under section 51, section 111 does not require making the proposed rural plan or amendment available for public consideration if the Minister makes a written summary available.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(14)Before making a regulation under this section, the Minister shall (a) if the regulation would have effect in a region, request the regional service commission to give its views on the regulation, (b) if the regulation is to be made under section 51 and would have effect in a rural district that has an advisory committee, request the advisory committee to give its views on the regulation, and (c) follow, with the necessary modifications, the procedure preliminary to the making of a by-law under section 111, except if the regulation is to be made under paragraph (1)(a), (b), (f) or (g). 125(15)Despite paragraph (14)(c), with respect to a zoning regulation under subsection (1) or a rural plan under section 51, the provisions of section 111 shall not be read as requiring the Minister to make available for public consideration the proposed rural plan or amendment if the Minister makes available for public consideration a written summary of the proposed rural plan or amendment.

objectives.objective: Recall where section 125 regulations are filed and the effect of filing on commencement.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Where must the Director file section 125 regulations, and is filing a condition for them to come into force?
objectives.studyAnswer: The Director shall file a copy of each section 125 regulation in the land registration office for every county where affected land is situated, but filing is not a condition precedent to the regulation coming into force.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(16)The Director shall file a copy of each regulation made under this section in the land registration office for every county in which any land affected by the regulation is situated, but the filing shall not be a condition precedent to the coming into force of the regulation.

title: Regulator assistance to the Board without party status

studySummary: For section 49.1, a regulator has the meaning assigned in the Financial and Consumer Services Commission Act. After a proceeding resulting from financial and consumer services legislation has commenced, and on application of the Board, a regulator who is not already a party may assist the Board without becoming a party, and the Board may receive and accept relevant information from that regulator whether or not it would be admissible in court.

title: Registration timing exceptions for leases, sale conveyances, and wills
mainQuestion: Which leases, sale conveyances, sheriff conveyances, and wills receive special registration timing treatment under section 19?
studySummary: Section 19(3) to 19(5) creates specific timing and registration-effect rules. Certain leases of three years or less with actual possession need not be registered and are not fraudulent and void merely because unregistered, but longer leases or leases without actual possession do not get that treatment. Official-capacity public-auction conveyances, sheriff conveyances under the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act, and wills are treated as valid against later purchasers or judgment creditors as if registered at the earlier specified time if they are registered within the stated deadlines.

objectives.objective: Recall the short lease exception from registration.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which leases need not be registered under subsection 19(3), and what leases are excluded from that exception?
objectives.studyAnswer: A lease for a term not exceeding three years need not be registered if actual possession goes along with the lease, and it is not deemed fraudulent and void merely because it is not registered. The exception does not apply to a lease for more than three years or to a lease where actual possession does not go along with it.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(3)No lease for a term not exceeding three years, where the actual possession goes along with the lease, need be registered, nor shall such lease be deemed fraudulent and void merely by reason of its not being registered; but this subsection does not extend or apply to any lease for a greater term than three years, nor to any lease where the actual possession does not go along with the lease.

objectives.objective: Recall the registration period and effect for official-capacity public-auction conveyances.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What is the registration deadline for an official-capacity public-auction conveyance to have sale-time validity against later purchasers or judgment creditors?
objectives.studyAnswer: If a person in an official capacity executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold at public auction pursuant to law, the conveyance is as valid against any subsequent purchaser or judgment creditor as if registered at the time of sale if it is registered within six months of the day of sale.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(4)Where a person in an official capacity executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold at public auction, pursuant to law, the conveyance, if registered within six months of the day of such sale, shall, as against any subsequent purchaser or judgment creditor, be as valid as if registered at the time of sale.

objectives.objective: Recall the registration period and effect for sheriff conveyances.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How does subsection 19(4.1) treat a sheriff conveyance registered within six months after execution?
objectives.studyAnswer: If a sheriff executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold by the sheriff under the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act, the conveyance is as valid against any subsequent purchaser or judgment creditor as if registered on the day of execution if registered within six months after that day.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(4.1)Without limiting subsection (4), if a sheriff executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold by the sheriff under the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act, the conveyance, if registered within six months after the day of its execution, shall, as against any subsequent purchaser or judgment creditor, be as valid as if registered on the day of its execution.

objectives.objective: Recall the registration periods and effect for wills.
objectives.guidedQuestion: When must a will be registered to be valid against later purchasers or judgment creditors as if registered immediately after death?
objectives.studyAnswer: A will has that effect if registered within six months after the testator death when the testator died within the Province, or within one year after death when the testator died without the Province.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(5)A will registered within six months after the death of the testator if he died within the Province, or within one year after death if he died without the Province, shall as against subsequent purchasers or judgment creditors be as valid as if it had been registered immediately after the death of the testator.

title: Transfer affidavit requirement and forwarding
mainQuestion: What affidavit must accompany a real-property transfer deed, and what must the registrar do with it after registration?
studySummary: A deed affecting the transfer of real property cannot be registered unless it is accompanied by a transfer affidavit containing the prescribed and listed information and made by an authorized person in the required form or to like effect. The registrar does not record the affidavit, but forwards it to the Executive Director of Assessment under the Assessment Act within thirty days after the deed registration date.

evidence.evidenceText: 19(6)No deed affecting the transfer of real property shall be registered unless accompanied by an affidavit of the transfer setting forth the true and actual consideration for which such property was acquired, the names of the parties, the location and description of real property and such other information prescribed by regulation

approximateLearningGoal: Recall the supporting materials and report contents required for a boundary-confirmation application.
title: Application materials and surveyor report content
mainQuestion: What supporting materials and surveyor report contents must accompany a boundary-confirmation application?
studySummary: In addition to the required plan of survey, a boundary-confirmation application must include the subsection 3(3) supporting materials, including field notes and a surveyor report from the signing surveyor, existing plans and conditionally available notes or reports, required registered instruments, any requested abstract of title, owner and interest information, any obtained consent, waiver, or agreement, and other helpful or requested material. The surveyor report must describe the issue, boundary history, evidence used, and reasons for accepting or rejecting other indicated boundary locations.

objectives.objective: Recall the surveyor-prepared materials accompanying the application.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which surveyor-prepared materials must accompany a boundary-confirmation application?
objectives.studyAnswer: In addition to the plan of survey, the application shall be accompanied by the field notes and a surveyor report conforming with subsection 3(4), prepared by the surveyor who signed the plan of survey.

evidence.evidenceText:
3(3)In addition to the plan of survey referred to in subsection (2), an application to confirm the location of a boundary shall be accompanied by

(a)
the field notes and a surveyor’s report in conformity with subsection (4), prepared by the surveyor who signed the plan of survey,

objectives.objective: Recall the documentary and ownership materials required with the application.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What plans, registered instruments, ownership information, consents, and other materials must accompany the application?
objectives.studyAnswer: The application shall include copies of any other existing plans showing the boundary, and if reasonably available, the field notes and surveyor reports for those plans; copies of all registered instruments in the Province relating to the boundary location and required by the Registrar General; any requested abstract of title; a list of names, mailing addresses, interests, and interest descriptions for current owners of the parcel and parcels sharing the boundary; any obtained consent, waiver of notice, and agreement to be bound; and any other helpful or requested information or documentation.

evidence.evidenceText:
(b)
copies of any other existing plans of survey on which the boundary in question is shown and, if reasonably available to the applicant, the field notes and surveyor’s reports relating to those plans of survey,

(c)
copies of all instruments registered in a registry office or a land titles office in the Province that relate to the location of the boundary in question and that are required by the Registrar General,

(d)
if requested by the Registrar General, an abstract of title in conformity with the directions of the Registrar General,

(e)
a list of the names and mailing addresses of all the current owners of an interest in the parcel in question and all the current owners of an interest in the other parcels sharing the boundary in question, including a description of the nature of the interest of each such owner,

(f)
any consent and waiver of notice obtained by the applicant and any agreement to be bound by an order of the Registrar General, and

(g)
any other information or documentation that would or could assist the Registrar General in dealing with the application or that is requested by the Registrar General.

objectives.objective: Recall what the surveyor report must contain.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must the surveyor report contain for the boundary-confirmation application?
objectives.studyAnswer: The surveyor report shall contain a description of the issue to be determined, a description of the boundary history, a description of the evidence used to establish the boundary location shown on the plan of survey, and an explanation of the reasons for accepting or rejecting the boundary location shown on other plans or indicated by other documentary evidence, physical evidence of earlier boundary lines, or boundary lines accepted by adjoining landowners.

evidence.evidenceText: 3(4)A surveyor’s report referred to in paragraph (3)(a) shall contain (a) a description of the issue to be determined, (b) a description of the history of the boundary in question, (c) a description of the evidence used to establish the location of the boundary as shown on the plan of survey, and (d) an explanation of the reasons for accepting or rejecting the location of the boundary as shown on any other plans of survey, as indicated by any other documentary evidence or as indicated by any physical evidence of earlier boundary lines or boundary lines that have been accepted by adjoining landowners.

title: Registrar General waiver of application requirements
mainQuestion: What may the Registrar General waive from the boundary-confirmation application materials, and on what terms?
studySummary: The Registrar General has discretion to waive any of the subsection 3(3) application-material requirements. Any waiver is subject to the terms and conditions the Registrar General considers appropriate.
